alignment.note: The Vulgate omits the entire departure clause (Greek Κἀκεῖθεν ἐξελθόντες, Peshitta ܘܟܕ ܢܦܩ ܡܢ ܬܡܢ 'and when he went out from there'), beginning instead with the teaching activity. This represents a major structural divergence, as the Vulgate conflates Mark 9:30 with 9:31, eliminating the geographical transition frame.

The Vulgate omits the journey-through-Galilee clause entirely (Greek παρεπορεύοντο διὰ τῆς Γαλιλαίας, Peshitta ܥܒܪܝܢ ܗܘܘ ܒܓܠܝܠܐ 'they were passing through Galilee'). The Latin tradition proceeds directly to the teaching content of verse 31, collapsing the narrative sequence and eliminating the spatial setting that both Greek and Syriac preserve.

The Vulgate omits the secrecy motif (Greek καὶ οὐκ ἤθελεν ἵνα τις γνοῖ, Peshitta ܘܠܐ ܨܒܐ ܗܘܐ ܕܐܢܫ ܢܕܥ ܒܗ 'and he did not want anyone to know about him'). Instead, the Latin text substitutes an entirely different verse (Mark 9:31), introducing teaching content not present in the Greek or Peshitta witnesses for this verse. This constitutes a major textual divergence involving verse-boundary conflation.

The Vulgate inserts the entire content of Mark 9:31 (Docebat autem discipulos suos... tertia die resurget 'Now he was teaching his disciples... on the third day he will rise') in place of the Greek and Peshitta text of 9:30. This represents a verse-conflation or alternative versification tradition in the Latin manuscript lineage, where 9:30 and 9:31 are merged under a single verse number with the geographical frame omitted.
